Triggers.value: Difficulty breathing or feeling short of breath

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Talking with others about the event or its aftermath
Open or exposed spaces where I feel vulnerable

Threat.value: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing
The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me

Negative Appraisals.value: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it
The people responsible have faced no consequences
The event happened because of the way I acted

issues.item: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: 'Body Shame' is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the profile for a civilian-in-war-zone trauma unless there is some indication of bodily violation, injury, or humiliation. The other selected items center on injustice, impunity, hypervigilance, dissociative/fragmented memory, and avoidance, but provide no supporting context for body-focused shame, making this item stand out as clinically mismatched.

issues.item: Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
issues.explanation: The Threat items emphasize pervasive current danger and hypervigilance (scanning exits, needing to stay alert at night), but the formulation specifically has Triggers → Threat inactive. In this profile, Triggers are concrete reminders such as car sounds and related media, yet the Threat items are generalized and not plausibly linked to those triggers; this makes the threat presentation feel disconnected from the trigger pattern.

vignette: At seventy-four, Dinh still carried the weight of his years as a civilian mechanic in a war-torn province. He remembered the day the supply road collapsed under sudden artillery, the sky filling with the roar of approaching aircraft, and his own lungs burning as he scrambled through choking dust. Decades later, any car backfiring on the interstate would immediately spike his breathlessness, while watching historical documentaries on television would instantly pull him back to that morning. Those sudden sensory triggers reliably fractured his recall, leaving him with only disjointed shards of the past rather than a continuous narrative. Because the memories felt so vivid yet incomplete, they actively drove his daily retreat: he stopped discussing the war with his wife, redirected his thoughts the moment a conversation drifted toward military history, and began avoiding the wide-open welding bays of his current machine shop. When the bay doors were raised and the afternoon sun flooded the concrete floor, the exposed expanse felt like a trap, so he quietly shifted to the narrow, partitioned workstations where he could keep his back to the wall. The disjointed, alien quality of his recollections kept his nervous system permanently activated, manifesting as relentless hypervigilance and an inability to quiet his mind before bed. He would lie awake until dawn, convinced that staying alert was the only way to survive an attack that could come at any moment. Because the events felt so unreal, he began to doubt his own competence, which gradually hardened into a fixed belief that he must have acted improperly and caused his own suffering. His fragmented recall repeatedly hijacked his present awareness, making a delivery truck's engine instantly trigger a wave of panic that mirrored the original ambush. He was certain that if he stopped monitoring his surroundings, the past would catch him completely unprepared, and that constant mental scanning only made ordinary environmental cues escalate into full-blown triggers without warning. His conviction that what happened was deeply unfair, that responsible parties faced no consequences, and that he alone was to blame steadily pushed him further into silence. That simmering sense of injustice continuously flooded his body with a constant sense of danger, keeping him perched on the edge of sleep and scanning every room as if hostiles might emerge. The lingering belief that the event was profoundly unaccounted for actively sharpened his reaction to everyday stimuli, turning routine car exhaust into a warning sign of imminent violence. He had come to interpret ordinary traffic noise not as coincidence, but as a deliberate provocation that demanded immediate internal withdrawal. In his Vietnamese-American home, family duty often meant enduring hardship silently, but Dinh found he could no longer swallow the weight of his unspoken years. By consistently redirecting his thoughts and avoiding open spaces, he prevented himself from processing the experience, which only left his memory more detached and inaccessible. His ongoing refusal to talk about the past or step into exposed areas slowly convinced him that the world remained fundamentally unsafe, reinforcing his conviction that the injustice stood unresolved and that he alone had to bear the guilt. His PCL-5 score of sixty reflected a life narrowed by relentless anticipation, where avoidance had become a self-fulfilling prophecy. Now, the tightening grip of that cycle finally forced him through the clinic doors. He hoped a therapist might help him untangle the knot of self-blame that kept him perpetually braced for a threat he could no longer outrun, desperate to reclaim the quiet stability he had once taken for granted.
